newsitem.title: UK: Softs Outlook-Cocoa and sugar may gain.
newsitem.headline: Softs Outlook-Cocoa and sugar may gain.

text.p: London white sugar is poised to hold much of its strength this week after last week's rally to a six-month peak, while cocoa may revisit the April 2 high on a positive technical picture.

But robusta coffee futures' prospects remained neutral, with the market showing little tendency to break either side of its range. Upside potential was capped by origin hedge sales, particularly by Indonesia.
But industry demand was limited ahead of the summer in the northern hemisphere, when roasting would take a seasonal dip.
July futures were likely to maintain their current range between $1,600 and $1,700 a tonne. A venture above $1,705, the April 21 high, would clear the way for a test of the last $1,800 peak.
On the downside, the main area to watch was the March 25 low of $1,535, a breach of which would take the market back to the $1,400 area.
However, traders said pre-Brazil frost season covering would help underpin the market.
"But the market is now performing as if there will be no frost," said one trader. "People were more wary last year than this year."

The end of the six-day Colombian truckers' strike took some steam out of the buoyant New York arabica futures market late last week. But positive technical indicators and persistent supply concerns might provide immediate support to New York.
In cocoa, the technical outlook seemed bullish, with most traders forecasting second-month July rising to the April 2 high of 1,065 stg per tonne.
If July closed at that level, some expected funds to start a buying spree that might push prices sharply higher. Next resistance stood near 1,080, a level last seen in August.
The main concern overhanging cocoa remained the low outright volume in the latest rise. Traders said most activity in that move up had been in switches.
Initial July support rested at 1,006 with stronger support near 980, the April 9 low.
Underlying fundamental support should come from speculation that shippers in Ivory Coast were having trouble fulfilling commitments for April and May contracts.
But analysts in Abidjan said on Thursday heavy April rains in Ivorian cocoa areas should favour mid-crop pod growth, which could ease any apparent shortages for shippers, some traders said.
Such debates should end and cocoa's direction should be clarified within the next two weeks, when Ivory Coast is expected to release export figures.
In white sugar, traders said they expected London's spot August contract to hold much of its strength after last week's rally.
But the nearby August/July arbitrage might come under selling pressure as it was likely to widen if New York's July contract edged towards support at 11.00 cents/lb.
August had surged to six-month highs as demand picked up and as traders feared being caught short in August when quality European supply could be tight.
The August/October spread should also command much attention from traders after last week's volatility, when it doubled to $10.00 in a matter of a few days.
Demand for raws, particularly from Russia and smaller amounts from China, had supported flagging prices.
"People are adjusting their attitudes -- they think the Russians are nibbling at a little bit. It just looks good," said one trader.
"I think people are just buying the rumour, hoping that the Russians are going to come and buy some more."
Although Russia had bought raw sugar to be refined internally, traders said, the bullish sentiment was still likely to spill over into London.
"If raws are being taken off the world market then people can still get bullish on the whites as there's less sugar around," said another trader.
